lead: A crystallizer is a vessel that creates supersaturation, holds the crystals in suspension while they grow, and removes or supplies the heat involved. Crystallizers are classified first by how they create supersaturation, then by how they keep the crystals moving and control their size. Their design rests on two balances: a mass balance for the yield and an energy balance for the cooling or heating duty, including the heat released as the crystals form.
prereq: You need the yield balance from Crystallization: solubility curves and supersaturation.

blocks.text: By the method of creating supersaturation there are four classes: cooling crystallizers, for solutes whose solubility falls steeply with temperature; evaporative crystallizers, which boil off solvent with heat supplied by steam, for flat-solubility salts such as NaCl; vacuum (adiabatic flash) crystallizers, in which hot feed enters a vessel held at low pressure, boils, and is cooled and concentrated by its own evaporation with no heat exchange surface; and precipitation crystallizers, where a reaction or an added antisolvent or salt (salting-out) lowers the solubility. Each may run batch or continuously.

blocks.text: The mixture of crystals and mother liquor in a crystallizer is the magma. Its solids content, often 20–40 %, is kept high enough to give a large crystal surface for growth, which keeps the supersaturation low.

The yield follows from the solute and water balances with saturated mother liquor, as for one stage: crystals P = solute in feed − solute left in the mother liquor, with evaporated water and hydrate water taken out of the liquor first. In a vacuum crystallizer the water evaporated is not chosen: it is fixed by the energy balance, so the mass and energy balances must be solved together.

Crystals themselves are nearly pure, because impurities rarely fit the lattice. The product's impurity comes mostly from mother liquor left on and between the crystals: a cake holding 5 % of its mass as mother liquor with 2 % impurity carries 0.1 % impurity when dried. Large, even crystals hold less liquor and wash better, which is one reason size control matters. Washing on the filter or centrifuge, and recrystallizing when needed, raise purity.

Most salts release heat as they crystallize from solution (the heat of crystallization, roughly the negative of the heat of solution). In a cooling crystallizer this heat must be removed together with the sensible heat of the feed:
cooling: Q = F c<sub>p</sub>(T<sub>1</sub> − T<sub>2</sub>) + P λ<sub>c</sub>      vacuum: V λ<sub>v</sub> = F c<sub>p</sub>(T<sub>1</sub> − T<sub>2</sub>) + P λ<sub>c</sub>
blocks.where: Q is the heat removed (kJ/h); F the feed (kg/h) of heat capacity c<sub>p</sub>, cooled from T<sub>1</sub> to T<sub>2</sub>; P the crystals formed (kg/h); λ<sub>c</sub> the heat of crystallization (kJ/kg, released); V the water evaporated and λ<sub>v</sub> its latent heat at the crystallizer temperature. In an evaporative crystallizer the steam supplies V λ<sub>v</sub> less the heat of crystallization and plus any sensible heating. More exact work uses an enthalpy–concentration chart.

blocks.text: In a cooling crystallizer the heat goes to cooling water through a jacket or coil, sized by Q = UAΔT<sub>lm</sub>. The cold wall is the most supersaturated place in the vessel and grows scale, so the temperature difference across it is kept small, often below 10 °C. In a vacuum crystallizer there is no cold surface at all: the boiling solution sets its own temperature through the pressure held by the condenser and ejector.

sections.h3: Design of batch and continuous crystallizers

blocks.text: A batch crystallizer is designed around its cooling (or evaporation) programme. Natural cooling is fastest at the start, when the solution is hottest, which drives supersaturation into the labile zone and makes fines. A controlled programme cools slowly at first and faster later, as the crystal surface grows, keeping supersaturation steady in the metastable zone; seeds are added just after saturation is reached. The batch time is set by the growth rate and the size wanted (ΔL = Gt).

A continuous crystallizer is sized by residence time: volume = volumetric feed × τ, with τ chosen so the dominant product size reaches the target, as worked out in Crystal size distribution and the MSMPR crystallizer. The heat duty sets the exchanger or condenser, and the magma density sets the circulation rate. Fines destruction (heating a stream of fines to dissolve them) and classified product removal are added when larger, narrower sizes are needed.

examples.question: 1000 kg/h of a solution with 30 mass% solute at 50 °C is cooled to 20 °C in a continuous cooling crystallizer. Solubility at 20 °C is 20 g per 100 g water; crystals are anhydrous. Take c<sub>p</sub> = 3.8 kJ/(kg K) and heat of crystallization 120 kJ/kg. Cooling water flows counter-current from 15 to 25 °C. Find the crystals, the heat removed, the cooling water and the area for U = 0.5 kW/(m² K).
steps: Feed: 300 kg/h solute, 700 kg/h water. Mother liquor holds 700 × 0.20 = 140 kg/h. Crystals P = 300 − 140 = 160 kg/h (53.3 % yield).
Sensible heat = 1000 × 3.8 × (50 − 20) = 114 000 kJ/h. Heat of crystallization = 160 × 120 = 19 200 kJ/h.
End differences: 50 − 25 = 25 K at the hot end, 20 − 15 = 5 K at the cold end. ΔT<sub>lm</sub> = (25 − 5)/ln(25/5) = 20/1.609 = 12.43 K.
examples.answer: 160 kg/h of crystals; 37.0 kW removed (14 % of it heat of crystallization); 3187 kg/h of cooling water; 5.95 m² of cooling surface.

examples.question: The same feed enters a vacuum crystallizer instead, flashing to 20 °C, where λ<sub>v</sub> = 2454 kJ/kg. Neglect boiling-point rise and heat losses. Find the water evaporated and the crystals.
steps: With V kg/h evaporated, the water left is 700 − V and the solute it holds is 0.20(700 − V). Crystals P = 300 − 0.20(700 − V) = 160 + 0.20V.
The vessel must be held near the vapour pressure of water at 20 °C, about 2.3 kPa, by a condenser and ejector.
examples.answer: 54.8 kg/h of water flashes off and 171.0 kg/h of crystals form, 11 kg/h more than in the cooling crystallizer, with no cooling surface to scale.

traps: The heat of crystallization is removed as well as the sensible heat; leaving it out undersizes the cooler (here by 14 %).
In a vacuum crystallizer the evaporation is fixed by the energy balance; solve mass and energy balances together.
A vacuum crystallizer has no cooling water on the solution side; the vapour carries the heat away to the condenser.
Salting-out is not a reaction: the added salt or solvent lowers the solubility; precipitation by reaction forms a new compound.
Magma is the whole suspension of crystals in mother liquor, not the mother liquor alone.

quiz.q: Classify crystallizers by the method of creating supersaturation.
quiz.a: Cooling, evaporative, vacuum (adiabatic flash, cooling plus evaporation) and precipitation (reaction, antisolvent or salting-out).

quiz.q: Why does a DTB crystallizer give larger crystals than a plain forced-circulation unit?
quiz.a: Its baffled settling zone draws off liquor carrying only fines, which are dissolved by heating and returned; removing excess nuclei leaves fewer crystals to share the solute, so they grow larger.

quiz.q: An evaporative NaCl crystallizer boils off 1000 kg/h of water at 100 °C (λ = 2257 kJ/kg). Neglecting the heat of crystallization and sensible heat, find the steam duty.
quiz.a: Q = 1000 × 2257 = 2.257 × 10<sup>6</sup> kJ/h = 627 kW; in practice multiple-effect evaporation or vapour recompression cuts the steam.

quiz.q: A continuous crystallizer needs a residence time of 2 h for the size wanted. Feed is 5 m³/h. Find the working volume.
Why is a controlled cooling programme better than natural cooling in a batch crystallizer?
quiz.a: Natural cooling is fastest at the start, when the crystal surface is smallest, so supersaturation overshoots into the labile zone and fines form. Controlled cooling starts slowly and speeds up as the surface grows, keeping supersaturation steady and the crystals larger and even.

quiz.q: Choose a crystallizer for 20 t/h of coarse ammonium sulfate, whose solubility changes little with temperature. Justify.
quiz.a: Flat solubility rules out cooling; evaporation is needed. A DTB evaporative or vacuum crystallizer suits a large continuous duty and, with fines destruction, gives a coarse product; an Oslo unit gives even larger crystals at higher cost. A Swenson–Walker or batch tank is too small and gives no size control.

beyond: Not for the exam. Mechanical vapour recompression lets an evaporative crystallizer reuse its own vapour as heating steam, cutting energy several-fold; it is standard in salt and zero-liquid-discharge plants. Continuous oscillatory baffled crystallizers are being adopted for drugs. Search for mechanical vapour recompression crystallizer and zero liquid discharge.

figure.caption: The two worked examples. Left: a jacketed cooling crystallizer removes 37.0 kW (sensible heat plus heat of crystallization) into 3187 kg/h of cooling water across 5.95 m², giving 160 kg/h of crystals. Right: in a vacuum crystallizer the same feed boils at 20 °C under about 2.3 kPa; 54.8 kg/h of vapour carries the heat away and the yield rises to 171.0 kg/h.
